splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on when actuarial assumptions must be finalized for calculating employer withdrawal liability under ERISA. The timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers owe, affecting billions of dollars in obligations across thousands of multiemployer pension plans. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require all assumptions to be locked in by that date.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be finalized by the end of the prior plan year (the statutory measurement date), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled while the supervisee is a fugitive, extending the court's jurisdiction to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release terms and that the judicially created fugitive tolling doctrine cannot extend the period of court-ordered supervision beyond the term specified in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prevents relitigating previously presented claims — in addition to § 2255(h)'s separate requirements. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are more strictly limited; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h). SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners bringing successive motions under § 2255, imposing a stricter gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners under § 2255, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on the circumstances under which candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The split affects whether disputes over election rules can be resolved before Election Day or must be deferred until after, with significant implications for mail-in voting and ballot-counting deadlines nationwide. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election laws that allegedly dilute lawful votes or alter election outcomes, recognizing a competitive injury sufficient for standing.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing to challenge election procedures before an election absent concrete, particularized injury beyond speculative vote dilution.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the federal Sentencing Guidelines that increase criminal penalties.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding criminal liability or instead apply the rule of lenity to resolve ambiguity in favor of the defendant. At least three circuits hold lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit held that deference prevails. Post-Loper Bright, this tension has intensified.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity, as an ancient canon of interpretation, takes precedence over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability without proper lawmaking.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary applies even in criminal contexts, allowing anti-defendant readings of ambiguous guidelines when the commentary is a reasonable interpretation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (requiring only one).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether 'and' in the safety-valve provision means defendants are disqualified from relief below mandatory minimums only if they meet all three listed criminal-history criteria, or if meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. The split leads to dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on jurisdiction.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they satisfy all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1's expansion of the guideline text.
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether Application Note 1 to the career-offender guideline — which adds conspiracy and attempt to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' — is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses. The split affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative — inchoate offenses included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline entitled to deference under Stinson and Kisor, so conspiracy and attempt qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text — inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its plain meaning, so conspiracy does not qualify as a controlled substance offense.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) encompasses state drug offenses involving substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a prior state drug conviction counts as a 'controlled substance offense' for guidelines purposes when the state criminalizes a substance not controlled under federal law. The Eighth Circuit holds no federal-law limitation applies, while other circuits require the substance to be federally scheduled. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: State-only substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines' reference to 'an offense under state law' broadly includes state drug offenses regardless of whether the substance is federally scheduled, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Substance must be federally scheduled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if it involves a substance also controlled under federal law, requiring a match between state and federal drug schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in law can support compassionate release, either alone or combined with other factors. Some circuits categorically prohibit such consideration, while others permit it. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this, but circuits like the Seventh have held it exceeds the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons warranting a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the terms of their imprisonment (such as transfer to prerelease custody) must proceed under habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241) or may bring civil rights claims.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions or terms of confinement — as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement — must be brought as habeas corpus petitions or may proceed as civil rights actions. This affects prisoner claims regarding BOP decisions on prerelease custody, First Step Act time credits, and similar matters. The Supreme Court has acknowledged but not resolved this split.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for fact/duration challenges; conditions may proceed as civil rights claims
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is exclusive only for challenges to the fact or duration of confinement, while conditions-of-confinement claims may proceed as civil rights actions under Bivens or § 1983.

positions.label: Habeas may also be used for conditions claims affecting custody terms
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is available for challenges to BOP decisions affecting custody terms, such as transfer to prerelease custody or application of earned time credits under the First Step Act.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly impose or increase a sentence upon revocation of supervised release to punish a defendant for the conduct that violated the conditions of release, as opposed to sanctioning the breach of trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to punish defendants for supervised release violations, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences may only address the breach of trust inherent in the violation rather than punish the underlying conduct. This affects hundreds of revocation proceedings annually.

positions.label: Punishment for violation conduct is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for the conduct that violated supervised release conditions, not just the breach of trust, placing this circuit at the extreme of the split.

positions.label: Revocation addresses breach of trust, not punishment for conduct
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of revocation of supervised release is to sanction the breach of trust, not to punish anew for the underlying violative conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the time limit for appealing a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil appeal deadline (30 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees — filed in a criminal case — is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of the appellate deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the fees motion is ancillary to the criminal case, but a minority view applies the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Rule 4(a) governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises from a criminal case, the shorter criminal appeal deadline under Rule 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held it belongs to the estate, while other circuits have held it belongs to the debtor. This affects homeowners who experience property appreciation during bankruptcy.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), coupled with the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a), means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by valuing estate property as of the original petition date, so post-petition appreciation remains with the debtor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether orders denying motions to seal documents containing private medical information are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable as a collateral order because medical privacy is a value of 'high order.' This creates a potential split with circuits that have taken a narrower view of the collateral order doctrine for sealing denials, limiting immediate appealability to a small set of recognized categories.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that medical privacy interests are sufficiently important that denial of a motion to seal medical records is a collateral order appealable under § 1291 because delayed review risks irreparable destruction of the privacy interest.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing denials generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's stringent requirements because the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated on appeal from final judgment or through other protective measures.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve differing approaches among circuits regarding liability standards for discrimination in hospitality and business establishments. The Court's review of the Second Circuit's approach suggests a circuit split on the applicable legal framework for such claims. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied a particular legal framework for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality establishments that the Supreme Court found sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Applied different standards for evaluating discrimination or unfair treatment claims against business establishments, creating the split that prompted SCOTUS review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
